Parties and figures

The Democrats

led by Yair Golan, a centre-left party, a merger of Labour and Meretz.

Yesh Atid

led by Yair Lapid, a centrist party running on a joint list, Beyachad or Together, with Nationalist Naftali Bennett.

Yashar!

led by Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff, a centre-right party.

Base
Secular Israelis (who make up around 45% of the Jewish-Israeli public). Those living in the wealthier part of the country, that is “Middle Israel” and Tel Aviv. Those in the suburbs or kibbutzim who are Ashkenazi, highly educated and middle-class. High-tech workers (an economically privileged group making up 10% of Israel’s workforce).

Origins
Labour Zionists founded Israel and led its governments until 1977, designing and dominating its institutions. Today, that liberal and socialist tradition looks increasingly anachronistic. The socialist economic model has been largely replaced by a neoliberal one and the once powerful labour union, the Histadrut, is now controlled by Likud.[1] The Democrats are their most direct successor. Yesh Atid is the heir to a more centrist tradition that arose in the 1980s to represent the secular middle class, defined by patriotism, diluted right-wing security positions, a cost-of-living agenda and hostility towards the ultra-Orthodox. On the right, Eisenkot comes from a long line of former security figures who join politics, promising heavyweight security credentials and competent governance.
Today’s Liberal Zionists emerged in 2019 in response to Netanyahu’s re-election. The camp was later energised and consolidated by the judicial overhaul in 2023, which mobilised thousands of Israelis to demonstrate week after week to safeguard liberal democratic institutions.

Summary
The Liberal Zionists are committed to Israel as a secular liberal democracy, with independent institutions, the rule of law and individual protections for its citizens, including Palestinian citizens of Israel. On Palestine, they adopt many of the Nationalist camp’s hawkish positions yet would be willing to advance a diplomatic settlement including a political process and regional normalisation. They are broadly Atlanticist and seek alliances with liberal Europe and bipartisan support in the US.
Together with Nationalists Bennett and Liberman, the Liberal Zionists are united by their fierce opposition to Netanyahu, earning them the nickname “anyone but Bibi” (rak lo Bibi). They promote a largely technocratic programme that promises to put national interests above personal interests with good governance (mamlachtiut), an end to corruption, a written constitution, term limits, a reversal of the judicial overhaul and a commission of enquiry into October 7th. The camp is vehemently secular and opposes the draft exemption for the ultra-Orthodox, while championing a political “covenant of those who serve”; that is, a government which includes neither the ultra-Orthodox nor Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Since the Nationalists cast the “left” as anti-Jewish and anti-Zionist, the Liberal Zionists have largely renounced leftism and colluded in their own delegitimisation. In practice, the Liberal Zionists trim the excesses of Nationalist and Religious Nationalist policies but do not fundamentally challenge them. They reject annexation and denounce settler violence but not the settlements themselves, distinguishing between expanding “status quo” settlements close to the Green Line and those deep inside the West Bank. Publicly, they back hawkish security policies and the use of overwhelming military force as deterrence, albeit tempered by restraint and diplomacy (see the strategy Eisenkot wrote for the Israeli military in 2015). Together with the Nationalists, they also support expanding the Abraham accords and military action against Iran.
Despite their liberal overtures, this camp is largely silent on the Israeli control of 5.6 million Palestinians in the occupied territories and has, at least publicly, abandoned the two-state project. At most, the three leaders promote “separation” from the Palestinians as a means of maintaining a Jewish demographic majority, much like their predecessors, from Ben-Gurion to Yitzhak Rabin.
To the left of the Liberal Zionist camp, a small non-Zionist and anti-Zionist Jewish minority emphasises full equality and an end to the occupation. This stream is represented by Hadash-Ta’al, a joint Jewish-Palestinian list, and has virtually no political power, winning just five seats in the 2022 election and generally declining to sit in coalitions.
